edits.definition: Material selection is matching the substance to the job by reading its properties first. A cooking pot needs a good conductor of heat with a handle that is not; a window needs transparency; a raincoat needs to be waterproof and insoluble; a hammer head needs hardness. The same object may need a compromise — a bicycle tyre must be flexible yet tough — and often the choice is between two candidates with opposite strengths (steel strong but heavy, aluminium lighter but costlier). Choosing well is therefore knowing properties, knowing the job, and weighing the two against cost and safety.

Combustion — burning — is a fast chemical change in which a substance combines with oxygen, releasing energy as heat and usually light: a candle's flame, LPG under a cooking pot, petrol in an engine, coal in a power station. The burning substance is the fuel, oxygen is the supporter, and the products are new substances (carbon dioxide and water vapour from a clean hydrocarbon flame). Combustion needs all three — fuel, oxygen and heat to start — and removing any one puts the fire out, which is exactly how we extinguish flames. It is chemistry's most useful reaction, and its most watched hazard.

Weather instruments translate the sky into numbers. The thermometer reads temperature; the barometer reads air pressure, whose falling needle warns of a storm; the rain gauge measures how much precipitation fell, in millimetres; the wind vane shows where the wind comes from and the anemometer how fast it blows; and the hygrometer reads the moisture in the air. Read together at fixed times, these tools turn 'how does the weather feel?' into records that can be compared, graphed and forecast — every weather station and satellite launch stands on these same first measurements.

Climate decides agriculture: each crop carries its own demands for temperature, rainfall and sunshine, and only regions that supply them can grow it. Rice wants heat and standing water, so it belongs to the monsoon plains; wheat wants cool winters; tea wants warm, constantly damp hill slopes; millets tolerate dry, chancy rain. Farmers work inside these limits — choosing the crop to suit the climate, or irrigating to make up the missing water — which is why the map of crops matches the map of rain, and why a shifting climate redraws the map of food.

India holds many climates inside one border because its land spans desert, mountain, plateau and sea. The Himalayan heights run alpine to arctic — Leh sees snow while Chennai sees summer; the northwest is arid, with Rajasthan's deserts and hot, dry air; the west coast and Northeast are among the wettest places on Earth; the northern plains swing from fierce summer heat to winter fog and cold; and the coasts stay warm and humid all year. Temperature, humidity and rainfall vary so widely across these belts that in the same season one region harvests a frozen landscape and another a dripping green one.

After the Mauryan Empire faded around 185 BCE, no single power held India: the Shunga dynasty ruled from Pataliputra over the northern heartland, regional kingdoms rose across the peninsula, and waves of newcomers — Indo-Greeks, Shakas and Kushanas — ruled the northwest, bringing Greek coinage and art that reshaped Indian styles. Trade flourished along the routes joining these kingdoms to Rome and Central Asia, Buddhism spread with that traffic, and its art flowered at Bharhut, Sanchi and in the Gandhara and Mathura schools. Politically fragmented, the era was culturally and commercially one of India's busiest crossroads.

Divisibility rules are shortcuts that tell whether one number divides another exactly — remainder zero — without doing the long division. The classics: by 2, the last digit is even; by 3, the digit sum divides by 3; by 4, the last two digits form a number divisible by 4; by 5, the number ends in 0 or 5; by 6, the tests for 2 and 3 both pass; by 9, the digit sum divides by 9; by 10, the number ends in 0. Each rule is really a fact about place value in disguise, and together they sort, factor and check numbers at a glance.

Two straight lines in a plane can stand in three relationships to each other. Parallel lines keep a constant distance forever — however far extended they never meet, like railway tracks. Intersecting lines cross at exactly one common point, forming four angles there. Perpendicular lines are the special intersecting pair that meets at a right angle of exactly 90° — the meeting of a wall and the floor, the crossing of graph paper. Every pair of non-identical coplanar lines is either parallel or intersecting, and 'perpendicular' names the intersecting pair's most useful angle.

A transversal is a line that cuts across two or more other lines at different points — and in doing so it creates eight angles whose relationships run a large part of geometry. At the two crossings, angles pair up as corresponding (same relative position), alternate interior and alternate exterior (opposite sides of the transversal, between/outside the lines), and co-interior angles on the same side. When the cut lines are parallel, each pair of corresponding angles is equal, each alternate pair is equal, and co-interior angles sum to 180° — the tests by which any diagram proves its lines parallel.

Volume measures how much three-dimensional space an object fills — how many unit cubes of 1 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm would pack inside it without gaps. It is the property behind capacity questions: water in a tank, sand in a pit, air in a room. Cuboids are counted by multiplying the three edges (length × breadth × height, in cubic units), cubes by side × side × side; liquids are measured in litres and millilitres, with 1 litre the space of a 10 cm cube. Two shapes can hold the same volume with very different outlines — volume counts the space, not the silhouette.

Probability measures on a 0-to-1 scale how likely an event is: 0 means impossible (no sun rises in the west), 1 means certain (a tossed coin shows heads or tails), and values between give the ratio of favourable outcomes to all equally likely outcomes — a coin's heads is 1/2, a die's six is 1/6, a face card 12/52. The closer to 1, the more confidently expected; closer to 0, the rarer. Probability cannot say which single throw wins — it says what fraction of many repeated throws to expect, which is why it is the mathematics of games, weather guesses and risk of every kind.

A pattern is an arrangement built on a rule — numbers rising by a fixed step (2, 5, 8, 11), shapes repeating in a cycle, a figure growing by adding the same piece each time, a design rotating through equal turns. The rule is the pattern's soul: it says exactly how the next member is made from the ones before, and once found, it predicts every future member without building anything. Finding rules in patterns trains the most useful mathematical habit there is — looking past the individual items to the relationship that generates them.

Matter is the name for everything that has mass and takes up space — the iron of a nail, the water of a glass, the air in a balloon (invisible, yet it fills space and weighs something). Matter exists in three common states — solid, liquid and gas — and is built from tiny particles arranged differently in each. Materials are matter put to use: particular kinds of matter chosen for their properties (hardness, flexibility, transparency, conductivity) and shaped into objects. So the chair is a material (wood) made of matter, and every material is some useful form of matter.

A chemical change is a transformation that makes genuinely new substances: the old material's particles re-arrange into different kinds of matter with new properties, and the original cannot be brought back by simple means. Milk turned sour, iron turned to rust, paper burnt to ash, food digested in the body, a cake baked from batter — in each case the new substance is there to stay. The tell-tale signs are a new colour, a gas given off, heat or light released, or a solid settling out of a solution; the change is usually permanent, because chemistry, unlike shape or state, does not undo itself.

The National Government — the Union Government seated in New Delhi — is the highest level of government in India, whose authority runs over the whole country and in matters of national importance: defence, foreign affairs, currency, railways, national highways and communications. It works through three branches that check one another: the Legislature (Parliament — Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) makes the laws; the Executive (the President, Prime Minister and Council of Ministers) implements them; and the Judiciary (headed by the Supreme Court) interprets them and rules on whether they respect the Constitution. Laws made here bind every state and citizen.

Weather is the atmosphere's condition at a particular place and moment — today's temperature, humidity, cloud, wind and rain, changing hour by hour. Climate is weather's long-term average: the pattern of temperature and rainfall a region shows over about thirty years of records. Kerala's climate is warm and wet even on a rare cool morning; Rajasthan's is hot and dry even after a cloudburst. The difference matters practically: weather decides what you do today, but climate decides what crops a region grows, what its houses look like and what its farmers plan for.

Subsistence and commercial farming are the two great purposes agriculture can serve. Subsistence farming feeds the farmer's own family first: small plots, family labour, simple tools, food grains and little left to sell — the pattern across much of rural India. Commercial farming grows for the market: larger holdings, machinery, irrigation, hired labour and cash crops — tea, coffee, cotton, sugarcane — raised to sell in national and international markets for profit. The same crop can belong to either world, and the difference lies in scale, capital and destination: eaten at home, or sold beyond the village.

India's neighbours are the countries that ring its borders: seven share its land boundary — Pakistan and Afghanistan in the northwest, China, Nepal and Bhutan across the Himalaya in the north, and Bangladesh and Myanmar in the east — while Sri Lanka and the Maldives lie across the sea to the south in the Indian Ocean. With them India forms the South Asian family: rivers, mountain passes and sea lanes tie their histories together, and much of their trade, culture and politics moves across these near borders — which is why neighbouring relations are the first chapter of India's foreign policy.

India's land borders are the lines where its territory meets that of its neighbours — about 15,200 kilometres of frontier running through every kind of land. In the northwest the border with Pakistan and Afghanistan crosses the Thar desert and the mountains of Kashmir; in the north the long Himalayan frontier with China, Nepal and Bhutan climbs through the world's highest ranges; in the east the borders with Myanmar and Bangladesh wind through forested hills and river plains. Border guarding forces police these lines, and where territory is disputed — as with parts of the China and Pakistan borders — the line's very course remains a live issue.

The Delhi Sultanate was the era from 1206 to 1526 CE when five dynasties in succession ruled large parts of India from Delhi: the Mamluk (Slave) dynasty, founded by Qutbuddin Aibak, who began the Qutb Minar; the Khalji dynasty, under which Alauddin Khalji expanded the Sultanate to its widest reach; the Tughlaq dynasty, whose experiments included Muhammad bin Tughlaq's capital shift and token currency; the Sayyids; and finally the Lodis, defeated by Babur in 1526 — an end that opened the Mughal age. Its three centuries fixed Delhi as India's seat of power, a position the city has held in one form ever since.
